news.title: Most Americans had no idea who he was. Republicans are making sure you know Hasan Piker’s name.
news.text:
Hasan Piker is an unlikely star for a negative ad campaign. He has never run for office and says he has no interest in doing so. He holds no leadership position in any political party. He has no political action committee. Most of the country has no idea who he is: In April, 60% of likely voters told Echelon Insights they had never heard of him.

That was before he started appearing in living rooms across the nation, in ads paid for by Republicans who want him to be one of the most famous men in Democratic politics — and before prominent Democrats, including House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, condemned him in an effort to distance themselves from a figure they fear is too polarizing to help them retake the majority in November.

Piker's read on why is not exactly modest. “They do see me as a threat,” he said in an interview for the latest episode of MS NOW’s “Clock It with Symone and Eugene,” “and that's precisely the reason why they're attacking me with regular frequency.”

There are other reasons too. “My worldview is also very provocative,” he said. His style? “Rather incendiary.” And then there’s the trove of clips to draw from.

Piker, 35, is a self-described socialist and “anti-imperialist” who talks about politics on Twitch for seven hours a day, five days a week — with 3.1 million followers, some 25,000 people watching at any given moment and eight years of unedited commentary available to anyone with a clipping tool. His audience, by his own annual survey, is 43% under age 30 and 62% boys and men — demographics Democrats lost badly in 2024, when Donald Trump took 56% of men under 30, up from 41% four years earlier, according to Tufts University’s Center for Information and Research on Civic Learning and Engagement.

Piker has been a presence in leftist politics for years, mostly from his chair, interviewing Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., and hosting Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., who joined his stream in 2020 to tell viewers to make a voting plan. This cycle, he got out of the chair — stumping with Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, canvassing with Melat Kiros in Denver and campaigning with Francesca Hong in Milwaukee. That has put him at the center of perhaps the most consequential midterm election in a generation and made him one of the most argued-about figures in politics.

Republicans have found a use for him. Democrats have not figured out what to do about it.

Now, with seven weeks left before an election, the argument over Piker has become a proxy for a harder one: whether a messenger who reaches the young men Democrats lost in 2024 is worth what he costs the candidates who have to answer for him.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=U4lZ0SwPDEs

Over an hour, Piker accepted nearly every factual premise put to him by MS NOW: that his audience is not representative of the overall electorate, that the base of the Democratic Party is Black voters, that Americans are less hostile in person than the internet suggests, that Hong, one of the candidates he campaigned hardest for, lost in part because she could not handle the national spotlight.

He granted all of it. What he did not grant is that any of it obliges him to say a single thing differently.

“My bet on this isn’t that I’m doing this just so Democrats can win elections,” Piker said. “I’m doing this because it’s true and I want people to understand and maybe even entertain a different perspective, even if they don't fully internalize it and fully understand it.”

“Is what you're doing helping people win?” my co-host, Symone Sanders Townsend, asked.

“My theory is that the anger and my beliefs are far closer to the majority position than the beliefs demonstrated by the national Democratic Party,” Piker said. “There's this disconnect with how the people perceive the national Democratic Party — and how the people perceive even, like, the liberal side of mainstream media — and what the desires of the masses are.”

https://www.instagram.com/p/DdXk5zaRS_b/?hl=en

Piker describes his goal earnestly. 

“I’ve always wanted to foment class consciousness in America,” he said. His diagnosis is that most working Americans do not identify themselves that way, and that this has allowed Republicans to fill a vacuum and redirect that anger toward marginalized groups.

He said he never wanted to be the center of political attention: “I cover the news first and foremost.” He started his career in media on “The Young Turks,” a popular left-wing commentary show, before leaving to start his own streams in 2018. That was his focus, he said, until he traveled to anti-ICE protests and No Kings rallies last year and started rethinking his role after talking to other demonstrators.

“They [were] increasingly frustrated with the feckless ineptitude demonstrated by Democrats in positions of power,” he said. “They were saying, ‘Where are our leaders? Why are they not doing anything?’”

The frustration is real. A Quinnipiac poll released last week found just 21% of voters approve of how Democrats in Congress are doing their jobs. But that same poll complicates Piker’s read of where the country thinks the fix is: Only 26% of voters consider themselves supporters of the Democratic Socialists of America, the group he is a member of and promotes. Among Democrats, that figure is about 59%.

Piker was candid about how little hard data informed his view of voters outside of his streaming audience. Asked what informs his understanding of voters’ views, he said much of it comes from travel and from strangers approaching him in public.

“It's anecdotal for the most part,” Piker said. “In certain instances it's just vibes-based, really. It's not, it's not hard-line data. But sometimes you have to, you have to put forth your beliefs regardless of whether or not they are going to be the most appealing.”

Polling of the broader electorate suggests that the vibes may be misleading him. Echelon found that 56% of Democrats want the party’s 2028 nominee to take the approach of figures such as Kamala Harris, Gavin Newsom and Pete Buttigieg, compared with 33% who preferred the more progressive approach of Sanders, Ocasio-Cortez and Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass. Black and Latino Democrats — whose votes will carry weight under the party's new presidential primary calendar — were far more likely than white Democrats to call themselves moderate rather than progressive.

Piker does not dispute that some of his views sit outside the mainstream.

Asked about his formulation that Israel is “a thousand times worse” than Hamas — is it provocation, or something he truly believes? — he said he believes it, and that Hamas' violence is born of an occupation going on for 80 years.

Sanders Townsend pressed: Does he understand that people hear that as an endorsement of violence?

Piker answered by arguing that state violence is made invisible while resistance to it is coded as chaos, and compared the situation to protesting police brutality: The tear gas is normalized, the leaf blower that pushes it back is not. It sounded to her, Sanders Townsend said, like he was making some kind of comparison between Hamas’ violence and nonviolent protest; as someone who has protested police, she rejected the comparison.

Piker calls his approach to discourse “agitative propaganda” and says it has two purposes: to force his opponents into stating their real positions, and to shock everyone else into seeing injustices he believes they have been trained to ignore. As such, his list of provocative and potentially offensive comments is long.

That is where his method collides with electoral reality.

Piker’s model is, in part, Donald Trump, who proved an inflammatory style can win a national election. The difference, of course, is that Trump is a candidate for office and can choose the risks he wants to take. Piker isn’t running for anything, and the candidates he supports campaign on a very similar policy platform to what Piker promotes, though sometimes without the purposeful agitation.

Piker acknowledges the difference and does not think it matters. He points to the shift in American opinion on Gaza over the past few years as proof that his method works: Say the unpopular thing early, absorb the punishment and wait for everyone else to arrive.

At the heart of Piker’s foray into electoral politics is the fact that the behavior and language that is acceptable in Twitch chats and online are still not acceptable in the larger political arena. The internet rewards intensity and heat. Elections require persuading people who do not already agree with you. Piker has mastered the first and is only now learning lessons of the second.

“I do think that I am being helpful,” he said. “I'm a lefty content creator in a very hostile and reactionary internet space. I'm constantly out there opposing right-wing ideas, opposing right-wing disinformation campaigns. Part of the reason why Republicans have identified me is not because I have incendiary comments that they can point to over and over again. Part of that is because they do see me as a threat, and that's precisely the reason why they're attacking me with regular frequency.”

Recently, Piker has started wearing suits. Mostly gone are the muscle tees from the streams that made him Twitch-famous. It's "respectability politics," he said. "I'm not going to stop with this, so I might as well make something more presentable for older white women."

He will change his clothes. He will not change a word.

news.title: 'Voters are deeply concerned.' Democratic 2028 hopefuls debate AI regulations
news.text:
Amid warnings from artificial intelligence developers that AI could destroy humanity, potential Democratic presidential candidates are calling for increased federal regulation and criticizing President Donald Trump’s dismissal of concerns about the fast-changing technology.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom, who has signaled interest in running, called on the federal government to "step forward with robust, national regulations that match the urgency of this moment" on Sept. 9 after signing bills to create a framework for independent third-party evaluations of AI systems, set standards for AI auditors and improve child safety protections for AI chatbots.

Democratic Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego sent Senate leaders a Sept. 9 letter asking to establish a Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence in 2027 and echoed that request in a Sept. 15 interview on MSNOW.

Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, a former proponent of data center development, signed an August executive order placing new restrictions on data centers, including requiring approval from local communities. Shapiro, who was on the short list to be former Vice President Kamala Harris' running mate in 2024, will also give a speech on AI policy on Sept. 17 in Pittsburgh.

“I’m very concerned about a White House that has just told these companies to run free and basically opposed any kind of meaningful regulation,” former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, said on NBC’s “Meet the Press” Sept. 13, referring to the Trump administration's resistance to calls for new AI regulation. Buttigieg said it is “deeply dangerous to Americans and the world” for the president and Congress to not act immediately. 

Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Georgia, who is the subject of growing 2028 buzz, said during a Sept. 13 rally for his reelection campaign that Americans are filled with dread by the “crushing weakness of our politics against the massive stakes of our times.”

“A capable president would move swiftly to secure and reassure the American people, rush inspectors into frontier labs, fortify the nation against bioterrorism, demand legislation from Congress, and lead the world toward an AI treaty,” he said.

Intra-party divisions

Harris praised a new push to connect AI industry leaders and Democrats seeking new regulations as “encouraging.” The effort, called Project Blueprint, is being run by Democratic megadonor Ron Conway’s venture capital firm SV Angel. The company hired Jay Carney, a former press secretary for President Barack Obama, to lead the project. 

“It is possible to heed the warnings of so many AI researchers and address safety concerns without sacrificing the technology’s benefits,” Harris wrote on X Sept. 14. “But time is running out; the federal government must act quickly.”

Members of the party’s liberal wing pushed back. Morris Katz, one of the strategists behind Zohran Mamdani’s successful 2025 New York City mayoral campaign, called her comment a “total misread.”

“The problem is the outsized influence of industry,” Katz wrote on X. “Take them on. Don’t serve as an accomplice.”

Adam Green, the co-founder of the Progressive Change Campaign Committee, warned against any effort to give AI companies a larger role in shaping the guardrails placed on their industry. 

“This is not a moment for kumbaya with big tech billionaires who know that they have already done bad things and are looking for government whitewashing and potentially bailouts,” Green told USA TODAY. “This is a potential repeat of the banking collapse.” 

Centrists in the party, however, argue Democrats must find the right balance between placing limitations on AI and embracing the technology’s potential. 

“If you want to be president of the United States, you’re going to have to chart a path that says we are pro-innovation, pro-technologies that are going to help people,” said Oliver Libby, a venture capitalist and Democratic donor and adviser. “But those things should be done within the bounds of strong, and hopefully national regulatory regimes.” 

Real solutions will come from bipartisanship, not the extremes of the two parties, said Liam Kerr, the co-founder of Welcome PAC, a group working to boost moderates’ influence in the Democratic Party. 

“The more educated voters become on this complex issue, the more they’re going to want people who can credibly say they’ll work with the other side to forge an enduring solution to a massive, complicated problem,” he said. 

Republicans walk a tightrope

Voters' AI fears turned existential on Sept. 8, when Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon announced his resignation and claimed that insiders believe AI could “kill us all by the end of the decade.” Coxon's viral posts, along with warnings from other researchers, have fueled the recent push for the federal government to step in.

Trump, an ally of the tech industry and an enthusiastic booster of AI and the data centers that power it, warned of “a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers” in a Sept. 14 Truth Social post.

"The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!" Trump wrote in the post.

However, some Republicans have embraced regulating the industry.

Missouri Sen. Josh Hawley, a leading Republican voice on stronger AI regulation and chair of the Homeland Security subcommittee on disaster management, announced Sept. 10 that the panel would investigate OpenAI after its bots launched an unauthorized hacking attack of rival company Hugging Face in July. Hawley said in a letter to OpenAI CEO Sam Altman that the inquiry will also cover "growing allegations of the existential risk of new AI products." (Though Hawley is often mentioned as a potential 2028 candidate, the senator told the Washington Examiner on Sept. 15 he has "no intention of running.")

Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas, who chairs the Senate committee that oversees AI, said he is working with Democratic Sen. Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota and GOP Senate Majority Leader John Thune to draft a bill to address potential biological or nuclear threats from AI.

"We cannot stick our heads in the sand and pretend this technology isn’t happening," Cruz, who ran for president in 2016 and hasn't ruled out another run, wrote on X on Sept. 9. "We need guardrails. But America needs to lead."

Vice President JD Vance, the 2028 GOP frontrunner, told reporters Sept. 14 that the administration wants to "regulate smartly." He also called on AI companies to "stop" if they're "building Frankenstein" during a Sept. 15 interview with the All-In podcast.

An issue up for grabs

A majority of American adults are more concerned about the impacts of AI – including the impact data centers will have on the environment and energy prices to the risk of job losses and data privacy concerns – than they are excited about its possibilities, according to an August Pew Research Center poll.

Voters haven't chosen one party to trust on the issue. A New York Times/Siena poll released Sept. 15 found that voters are split on which party they trust more to address AI and data centers, with 42% saying Republicans and 40% saying Democrats, within the poll’s margin of error. Another 18% said they didn’t know. 

“If data centers are the issue of the midterms, then AI more broadly is going to be the issue of 2028,” Ravi Mangla, a spokesperson for the progressive Working Families Party, told USA TODAY. “Candidates are going to be judged by how seriously they’re taking the issue and how close they are with the tech industry.”

New groups are forming to help shape Democratic policies toward a unified vision. New York Assemblymember Alex Bores, an AI regulation advocate who lost a June congressional primary after being targeted by millions in AI super PAC spending, recently launched Who Decides, a proposed $30 million effort aimed at encouraging Democrats to run on a common AI safety agenda. 

Alums of Hillary Clinton and independent Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders’ 2016 presidential campaigns co-founded Tomorrow Together Action, a group that plans to spend $10 million during the midterm elections to help House candidates in swing states who support limits on data center construction, as well as data privacy and child safety regulations. 

“Voters are deeply concerned that they’re losing control over the decisions that matter in their life to a technology controlled by a small group of billionaire executives,” Jesse Ferguson, a Democratic strategist who presented at a recent gathering hosted by Tomorrow Together Action, told USA TODAY. “It’s a question of who controls the decisions in your life – that’s where voters are, and that’s where Democrats can meet them.”

The Banker Faced with a Canada's Sovereignty Heist

Behind the scenes, the Canadian Armed Forces are quietly bracing for impact. Strip away the bureaucratic jargon, and this amounts to conceding to a quick U.S. military occupation, relying instead on a long-term insurgency designed to make the occupation as bloody and costly for the Americans as possible. This is a catastrophic compromise. Allowing an American corporate-military apparatus to capture Canada's sovereignty would completely unbalance global geopolitics, throwing the world into a permanent, totalitarian AI police state.

If Canadians do not want to spend the coming decades living under an American military occupation defined by domestic drone warfare, the Carney government needs to start being frank with the public immediately. The current strategy of preparing a reactive, back-pocket insurgency must be dumped. Instead, Canada must adopt the "Total Society Defence" model pioneered by highly resilient nations like Sweden, Finland, and Israel.

Carney must stop treating Canada like a bank manager hiding from bank robbers. He must explicitly inform Canadians that the U.S. military now poses an active existential threat to Canada's sovereignty. By shifting to a total defence framework, Canada can openly mobilize a national territorial defence force exceeding 400,000 citizens stationed strategically across every province and territory. Only by transforming the entire population into a visible, permanent deterrent can we hope to extinguish the predatory calculations of the dark forces looking north, and preserve our nation before the border vanishes forever.

The Anatomy of Trump 2 and the Death of Canada's Sovereignty Restraint

To understand why a military conflict with our closest ally has shifted from an unthinkable absurdity to a mathematical certainty, one must dissect the psychological mutation of the American executive branch. During his first term, Donald Trump’s disruptive foreign policy was still bound by the residual friction of institutional norms—what Premier Doug Ford and continental diplomats relied upon as the internal "brakes" of the American state apparatus. There was a transactional predictability to the madness.

In his current incarnation, however, Trump 2 operates completely unmoored from historical alignment. The "apparition of Trump" represents the total triumph of pure, unadulterated ego over systemic governance. In this state, treaties like the USMCA are not sacred covenants but minor inconveniences to be torn up whenever the domestic resource furnace requires more fuel.

When Trump muses on social media about absorbing Canada or maps surface depicting the "United States of North America," the Canadian political establishment dismisses it as standard internet performance. This is a fatal diagnostic error. These spectacles are the ideological conditioning mechanisms for an American populace that will soon be asked to cheer on the unilateral securitization of Canada’s resource base.

The underlying driver is not ideological; it is existential resource depletion. The American southwest is running out of water, its industrial grid is starving for critical minerals, and its military planners are terrified of Chinese and Russian naval expansion in an iceless Arctic. Canada sits atop the largest real estate jackpot of the 21st century. To assume that a Washington ruled by "dark forces" of pure ego will respect a border drawn in 1846 while the rest of the planet burns is an act of collective national suicide.

The Failure of the Banker’s Deterrent

Mark Carney’s entire prime ministership has been an exercise in trying to out-monetize a geopolitical crisis. Lock-step with his ongoing Canada Investment Summit, where he is frantically pitching $1 trillion in sovereign projects to global asset managers, Carney views national survival through a balance sheet. His strategy is simple: weave a financial and technological web so dense, involving European and Asian capital, that the Americans would find an invasion too economically disruptive to execute.

This explains his desperate trip to Europe to secure a unique alliance with the European Union, positioning Canada as the ultimate partner. It explains the frantic, 9-day ultimatum handed to Volodymyr Zelensky to procure millions of battle-tested Ukrainian FPV drones. Carney wants an automated defence grid—a technological moat of autonomous algorithms and drone swarms that can guard the border while Canadians continue their business as usual.

But a bank manager cannot deter a cartel with a better alarm system. When Carney treats Canada’s sovereign territory as an "asset class" to be protected by outsourced supply chains, he miscalculates the psychology of the predator. Trump’s political-military-industrial complex does not care about market disruption; it thrives on it. A tech-only deterrent consisting of unbuilt drone fleets and non-binding Security and Defence Partnerships with distant European nations will be stepped over in the first forty-eight hours of a synchronized emergency.

Paving the Way for the Occupier

The most tragic irony of Carney's current infrastructure push is that he is essentially building the logistics network for an occupying U.S. military force. By prioritizing highly streamlined, integrated transportation corridors, deep-water ports, and centralized energy grids without an accompanying defence shield, Carney is laying down the exact blueprint required for an American blitzkrieg.

An invader does not want to rebuild a broken territory; they want a turn-key operation. Carney's massive infrastructure plans are perfectly optimized asset packages that an American military administration could co-opt within forty-eight hours. Unless Canada can physically intimidate the Americans from crossing the border through the sheer scale of its standing army, our domestic nation-building will simply serve as a welcoming gift to the Pentagon.

To the pure-ego apparatus steering Washington, Canada’s unpeopled, tech-dependent grid is not a deterrent—it is an open invitation. This vulnerability has not gone unnoticed south of the border. Public figures, pundits, and members of the Trump circle have repeatedly made sarcastic remarks questioning whether Canada "even has an army." These jeers expose a dangerous reality: Washington does not view Canada as a sovereign military entity, but as an undefended geographic buffer.

To shatter this perception, Canada must immediately abandon its minimal, boutique force posture and construct a massive, World War II-size army. In the arena of hard power, numbers are the only currency that commands respect. An overwhelming influx of standing personnel is the most essential element of any true sovereignty-focused nation-building plan. If the Americans know they will face a massive wall of physical resistance, the predatory calculation changes from a swift corporate restructuring to an unsustainable quagmire.

The Fallacy of Overseas Insurgency Models

The current defence planning, centred around an "asymmetrical warfare" contingency, is fundamentally flawed. Canada is not Afghanistan or Vietnam. We are not located across an ocean, insulated by thousands of miles of hostile terrain and disconnected from the invader's logistical base. Canada shares a contiguous, unfortified 8,891-kilometre border with the world's most advanced military superpower. Our major population centres, economic engines, and communication backbones sit within an hour's drive of that line.

Attempting to rely on asymmetrical warfare as a primary strategic focus under these geographic conditions is foolhardy. In an interconnected, modern Western state, a post-occupation guerrilla campaign would mean the complete, high-casualty devastation of Canadian cities. It would result in a brutal, fruitless conflict where our internal infrastructure is weaponized against our own population by an omnipresent American surveillance apparatus.

The only constructive purpose of asymmetrical warfare is to use it as an integrated element of a Total Society Defence framework. In a proper defensive doctrine, asymmetrical tactics are not a fallback option after the conventional military collapses; they are an active strategy used to throw the adversary off-centre. By deploying decentralized, asymmetric units alongside a massive standing territorial force, Canada can disrupt the enemy's logistics, sever their communications, and create tactical vulnerabilities that our main territorial defence forces can exploit to maintain sovereign control.

Why Carney's Nation-Building Plan is Built on Sand

A country cannot engage in nation-building if it is on the verge of being conquered.

Carney has spent months selling Canadians on an ambitious domestic economic transformation—a master ledger of clean energy corridors, digital innovation centers, and critical mineral extraction zones. Yet, by omitting an existential security architecture, Carney’s grand design amounts to setting the table for an uninvited guest. A financial architect can draft the most lucrative balance sheets in the world, but in a raw geopolitical landscape dominated by a predatory southern neighbour, an undefended asset is simply an asset waiting to be seized.

Carney’s most glaring strategic blunder is his refusal to make a Total Society Defence framework the absolute centrepiece of his national agenda. Without an overwhelming infusion of armed, trained personnel rooted in every municipality from coast to coast to coast, any talk of long-term economic sovereignty is an exercise in pure delusion.

Instead of relegating that proposal to academic archives or diluting it into toothless volunteer initiatives, that plan should have been militarized and expanded into a full National Territorial Defence Force of over 400,000 active citizen-soldiers.

A serious prime minister does not plan for how his citizens will hide in the bush; he organizes them so no hostile power dares to cross the border in the first place.

Churchill: The Northern Fortress and Epicentre of Sovereign Power

Nowhere is the collision between Carney’s commercial balance-sheet approach and existential defence needs clearer than in the rapid development of the Port of Churchill. Churchill provides tidewater access that dramatically shortens transatlantic trade routes to European ports.

In a crisis where southern borders and the St. Lawrence Seaway could be choked off by American naval and air blockades, Churchill is Canada's only secure, deep-water oceanic artery directly connected to European allies. Under a Total Society Defence doctrine, Churchill must be radically expanded from a mere infrastructure junction into the absolute epicentre of Canada’s new military defence capabilities.

To secure this subarctic fortress, the command structure must be completely decentralized and placed directly into the hands of Indigenous and Inuit commanders whose ancestral sovereignty over the land is absolute. Under their direct guidance, the military infrastructure at Churchill must undergo an unprecedented re-tooling:

Canada didn’t wait out a multi-year procurement lifecycle; it completely re-tooled its economy to push back against Hitler, constructing over 800,000 military vehicles, 16,000 combat aircraft, and a massive merchant marine that proved indispensable in liberating the Netherlands and turning the tide of the war.

Today, Canada finds itself paralyzed by multi-decade procurement loops and bureaucratic indecision. We cannot afford to wait years down the road for theoretical deliveries of customized, complex weapons systems. A Total Society Defence model demands immediate military preparedness.

The Carney government must bypass standard peacetime acquisition frameworks to launch immediate, emergency purchases of guns, ammunition, heavy anti-armor artillery, and ready-to-deploy fighter jets right now off the global market. In a resource confrontation driven by an unstable superpower, the only hardware that functions as a deterrent is the hardware currently sitting in Canadian hangars and armouries.

Immediate preparedness requires an absolute embargo on American defence suppliers. Canada's emergency procurement must look exclusively to independent European and Asian suppliers capable of delivering immediately survivable hard power.

Unlike platforms burdened by American supply chains, these aircraft offer complete sovereign control over source code and targeting arrays. On the ground, Canada requires an instant influx of armoured vehicles and heavy anti-aircraft infrastructure that can operate entirely independent of GPS. Alberta and Saskatchewan: Energetic Assets, Heavy Transport, and Ballistics

Manitoba: Precision Engineering, Aerospace Re-Shoring, and the Churchill Bastion

Manitoba’s central position makes it an ideal, secure hub for deep-tier component manufacturing, structural composite repair, and subarctic port operations.

Atlantic Canada: Naval Repair, Coastal Radar, and High-Explosives

The Atlantic provinces must harden our eastern littoral boundary, turning every port and industrial site into a naval bastion.

The Territories: Arctic Survival, Pickets, and Deep-Terrain Support

By transforming municipal emergency actors into active components of the National Territorial Defence Force, the country erases the vulnerability of a soft underbelly. Radical Transparency: A Total Society Defence model requires Prime Minister Carney to stop concealing the truth from Canadians. He must drop the comforting economic bromides of the Canada Investment Summit and admit openly that a military invasion is foremost on his mind.A Prepared National Consciousness: Many Canadians—including those already leaving Florida in anticipation of a rupture—can already sense the imminence of a continental shift. Our national consciousness is primed for mobilization; the public understands that we must act collectively to save lives rather than slip into a bloody and fruitless domestic conflict.Mass Kinetic Deterrence: The sheer arithmetic of occupying a nation defended by 400,000 mobilized, anti-tank and anti-drone equipped citizens completely shatters the operational feasibility of an American rapid occupation.Decentralized Urban Bastions: Rather than falling within hours to cyber decapitation, every major metropolitan corridor becomes an unassailable defensive redoubt managed by municipal units that do not rely on central direction from Ottawa.True Nation-Building Through Shared Duty: You cannot foster national cohesion through corporate subsidies and public-private partnerships alone. True civic resilience is forged when the entire population shares the collective responsibility of physical survival.

The choice before us is binary. We can continue to let a technocratic government manage our decline, treating an inevitable American foreclosure like a bad corporate restructuring. Or we can reclaim the divine spark of our collective humanity, organize our society from the ground up, and build a nation so thoroughly resilient that no predator, no matter how blinded by ego, would ever dare to cross the line.

news.title: Frail Mitch McConnell appears to need assist from fellow Republicans after he nearly votes wrong way in Senate
news.text:
Sen. Mitch McConnell appeared frail and required assistance from a fellow Republican senator at a committee hearing on Wednesday, two days after returning to the Hill for the first time since his hospitalization in June.

The Kentucky senator was at a meeting of the Senate Committee on Agriculture when his name was repeatedly called by a clerk recording the votes. Sen. John Boozman, a Republican from Arkansas, leaned in and instructed him to say “aye”.

McConnell then raised a finger and said, “aye,” and the votes continued.

The moment was quickly picked up online by Democrats who said that the senator had almost mistakenly voted with the wrong side.

“Republicans have to instruct Mitch McConnell to vote "yes" on a bill after he nearly votes "no" with Democrats,” wrote one account affiliated with the Democratic National Committee (DNC) and former vice president Kamala Harris.

Leaving the committee meeting afterwards, McConnell ignored questions from reporters outside as he was quickly wheeled away by aides.

The moment comes just two days after the senior Kentucky senator and former leader of the Republican conference returned from a months-long absence. He was hospitalized in June after a fall, and then developed pneumonia, according to statements released from his office. His return to Washington followed weeks in a rehabilitation center.

He smiled and gave a thumbs-up to reporters as he was wheeled by aides out of his D.C. home on his way to the Senate on Monday, but did not take questions from reporters or respond to shouted inquiries. Spectators and online viewers noted that he seemed to stare straight ahead, his mouth partially agape.

He hasn’t given an on-camera statement at length since his hospitalization. Before returning to Washington, Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear repeatedly urged his office to release a video of the senator talking about his recovery, but was rebuffed.

The Independent reached out to the senator’s office for comment.

At 84, McConnell is in his last term in the Senate. He announced last year that he would not stand for re-election, shortly after stepping down as leader of the Republican Senate conference and allowing his close ally Sen. John Thune to take over.

A former sufferer of childhood polio, McConnell has suffered repeated falls before, including on Capitol Hill, and over the past year has typically used a wheelchair to get around the Hill with the assistance of aides. One of the falls he suffered in 2023 occurred in public at Washington’s Reagan airport and was described as a “face-plant”.

Age has become a serious point of contention in Washington and particularly on Capitol Hill, where aging lawmakers in both chambers have faced accusations of remaining in office long after they are unable to effectively serve. Instances of such lawmakers suffering from bouts of confusion or disorientation have been reported involving members of both parties.

McConnell is no stranger to these concerns himself and alarmed many in the media and in the Senate itself when, in two moments within a few days of each other in the summer of 2023, he appeared to freeze up and be unable to speak at two news conferences on the Hill, surrounded by his colleagues and journalists.

On Monday, he described his recovery process after his latest hospitalization as sometimes frustrating, but said he was glad to be back in Washington.

“Today, I’ll cast my first Senate vote since I took a bad fall back in June. I’m really looking forward to being back on the Senate floor and seeing my colleagues,” said McConnell in a statement released to news outlets.

“My recovery has been a long and often frustrating process, and the lingering effects of childhood polio haven’t made it any easier. I’m still not quite back to 100%, but I’ve assured Leader Thune that, as I continue with physical therapy on the advice of my doctors, I will do my best to be present for tough votes when our Conference needs me,” his statement continued. “Elaine and I are very grateful for all the continued well wishes from our fellow Kentuckians, and I’m glad to get back to more of business as usual on their behalf this month.”
news.summary: McConnell is accused of nearly voting with Democrats by mistake at Agriculture committee meeting

news.title: Kamala Harris to campaign with Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan
news.text: Former Vice President Kamala Harris will campaign with Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan next week, a spokesperson for Harris confirmed to NBC News on Wednesday. El-Sayed, a former public health official, faces one of the most competitive Senate races in the country this year against former Rep. Mike Rogers. “Vice President Harris looks forward to returning to Michigan to help turn out the vote in this critical state. While there, she will highlight the issue of Black maternal health, joined by Dr. El-Sayed,” Harris spokesperson Eduardo Negrón said in a statement. “It is critical we flip the Senate so we can bring down prices and stand up to Donald Trump’s corruption.” Sen. Gary Peters, D-Mich., is retiring, and Democrats are seeking to hold on to his seat and potentially gain a Senate majority by flipping Republican-held seats in other states. Meanwhile, Republicans face headwinds like inflation and an unpopular war in Iran as they aim to maintain or expand their control of the Senate. Harris, who lost to Donald Trump in the 2024 election, endorsed El-Sayed in August after he won a competitive primary against Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens. Roxie Richner, a spokesperson for El-Sayed, told NBC News on Wednesday that “Abdul is thrilled to welcome Vice President Harris to Michigan for a conversation about improving Black maternal health and bringing down healthcare costs.” Richner added: “He looks forward to hearing directly from Black women and healthcare providers and discussing how he’ll continue that work in the Senate. There’s no better choice for Michiganders than Abdul when it comes to making healthcare more affordable, and he’s grateful Vice President Harris will join him in spreading that message.” Michigan has been a competitive battleground state in statewide and national elections for years. In 2028, it will be the fifth state to vote in the Democratic nominating contest for the presidential election. Harris has decided to campaign there amid speculation that she may run for president again in two years. In 2024, Trump beat Harris in Michigan by less than 2 percentage points on his way back to the White House. The same year, Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., beat Rogers in a Senate race by less than 1 point. Negrón added that while she is in Michigan, Harris will also meet with local elected officials and faith-based leaders. The race between El-Sayed and Rogers has gotten increasingly nasty in recent weeks. El-Sayed has targeted Rogers for accepting corporate donations, repeatedly accusing him of representing corporate interests. Alongside a video highlighting Rogers’ acceptance of campaign donations from pharmaceutical companies, El-Sayed wrote on X that Michiganders “are *literally* sick of Mike Rogers’ corruption.” In another post accusing Rogers of pushing to raise the retirement age nationally, El-Sayed wrote, “He’s a corrupt coward who cares only about his and his donors’ profits and nothing about people.” On the other side of the aisle, Vice President JD Vance has called El-Sayed “evil,” telling people at an event in Michigan last month, “I realize that there’s something about Abdul El-Sayed that is very, very evil and on the rise in the United States of America today.” El-Sayed has faced backlash for having accepted support from and campaigned with Twitch streamer Hasan Piker during the Democratic primary campaign. Republicans have sought to tie Piker’s past controversial comments about the 9/11 terrorist attacks to El-Sayed, who has disavowed them. Piker has also apologized for the remarks. El-Sayed, who would be the first Muslim U.S. senator, has accused Republicans of Islamophobic attacks against him. Shortly after his primary victory, the National Republican Senatorial Committee posted a video on X calling him “radical” and “dangerous,” using his full name, Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed. news.title: Republicans Get Warning Sign as Four 'Safe' Seats Shift Toward Democrats
news.text: Sabato’s Crystal Ball shifted eight races toward Democrats, including four previously thought to be safe GOP seats, on Wednesday—the latest warning sign for Republicans ahead of the November midterms. The changes come as Democrats are hoping to expand the battleground to compete in more conservative areas in this year’s elections. President Donald Trump’s approval rating has slipped to record lows in the latest polls amid growing frustration over the economy and cost of living. Democrats believe that could give them opportunities to flip more seats in Congress this year, even in states and districts that backed Trump by large margins in 2024. Democrats have also expanded their polling lead in the past few weeks. Democrats held an 8.6-point lead in RealClearPolitics’ aggregate of generic ballot polls. That’s the largest lead they’ve had so far this cycle and represents nearly a two-point leftward shift from one month earlier, when their lead stood at 6.8 points. That average is also identical to Democrats’ popular vote victory in 2018, when they rode a “blue wave” to flip more than 40 seats in the House of Representatives. Which Seats Changed in Sabato’s Crystal Ball New Ratings? The following seats shifted in the latest ratings from Sabato’s Crystal Ball: These sorts of seats could present Democrats with chances to cut into the GOP majority to establish a greater majority in a “blue wave” national environment. Many of these districts voted for Trump by double digits or have a history of voting. If Democrats make these races competitive, it would be a sign of a stronger blue wave. Currently, Republicans hold a slim majority with 218 seats compared to Democrats’ 214 seats and one independent, so Democrats only have to flip a handful of seats to win a majority. But winning tougher races would be beneficial, giving them more room for defections on key legislative priorities. Kyle Kondik, managing editor of Sabato’s Crystal Ball, wrote in the update that Republicans are facing an “enthusiasm problem” ahead of November, and that an effort to motivate the base by holding a convention in Texas “does not as of yet appear to be paying dividends.” “Those waiting for a Republican recovery in the polls will have to keep waiting, and the wait may be for Godot,” he wrote. “The post-Labor Day period has seen the Democrats generally doing well in surveys. The most-watched one was the New York Times/Siena University House generic ballot poll released Tuesday morning: Democrats were up 8.5 points.” Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee Communications Director Courtney Rice told Newsweek that Americans are “sick of rising prices and broken promises, and they’re ready to elect Democrats to the House Majority in November.” “While House Republicans are stuck trying to defend rising gas prices and the war in Iran, Democrats are on offense and poised to win in districts that voted for Trump by double digits,” Rice said. Newsweek also reached out to the National Republican Congressional Committee for comment via email. Democrats Gain in Safe Republican Seats Four of the shifts came in seats previously not viewed as competitive. Republicans are still favored in these races, but they are now viewed as being more engaged by the elections forecaster. “Things may end up bad enough for Republicans that we might see upsets in some places we don’t expect,” Kondik wrote. Here is a look at where things stand in each of these races. Arkansas’ 2nd District Republican Representative French Hill is facing a challenge from Democrat Chris Jones, an engineer and former gubernatorial candidate, in a Republican-leaning district. The district is based around Little Rock, a Democratic city, but also includes more conservative, rural areas across the central region of Arkansas. It backed Trump by nearly 16 points in 2024. Jones has received the endorsement of former Vice President Kamala Harris, but it’s not clear that national Democrats are prepared to invest in this seat. However, Republicans have begun putting money into this seat. “Hill recently benefited from about $400,000 in outside spending from a new Republican Super PAC, a development reported by Politico that raised our eyebrows a bit in a Trump +15ish district,” Kondik wrote. Nevada’s 2nd District This Nevada district has started to garner some attention, despite the fact that it backed Trump by 14 points in 2024. The vast district includes large swaths of rural areas in the northern part of the state, but many voters live in the Reno and Carson City areas. Historically, it has a Republican lean and has been represented by Republican Representative Mark Amodei since 2011. Amodei, who has overperformed other Republicans in the district, is retiring at the end of the term. His retirement leaves the seat open and has driven up Democrats’ hopes that they could pull off a surprise victory. A recent poll showed a closer race than expected, but still found a large number of voters are undecided. The GBAO poll, sponsored by a Democratic group, Nevada Alliance, found Democrat Teresa Benitez-Thompson, the former leader of the Nevada Assembly, with a single-point lead over former Air Force Lieutenant Colonel David Flippo, 38 to 37 percent. Independent American Party candidate Lynn Chapman also received 14 percent in the poll. It surveyed 500 likely voters from August 31 to September 3 and was first reported by The Nevada Independent. New York’s 21st District Republican Representative Elise Stefanik has won by large margins in this district, based around North Country. Once a more competitive area, the region has swung rightward over the past decade, backing Trump by more than 20 points in the last election. But Stefanik’s retirement has brought new attention to the seat. Businessman Anthony Constantino, a Republican, and Democrat Blake Gendebien, a dairy farmer, are running to succeed her in the House. A new poll of the district gave Constantino a modest lead. The Public Policy Polling/The Bench survey showed him up 5 points, 48 percent to 43 percent. It surveyed 557 registered voters from September 9 to 10, 2026, and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.2 percentage points. Blake Gendebien has received support from the Blue Dog PAC, a coalition supporting moderate Democrats. He told Newsweek in February 2025, when he was running for a special election that was canceled after Trump pulled Stefanik’s nomination to become United Nations ambassador, that Trump’s tariffs could make the district, which has close ties to Canada, more competitive. "We buy 80 percent of our potash fertilizer from Canada. This will impact the North Country and the entire United States. Corn, soybeans, and also forage, alfalfa, we require it. We need that fertilizer," he said at the time. "If there's a 25 percent tariff on that, all of our food is going to get more expensive. There's no way around it." Ohio’s 10th District This district is, in theory, more competitive than the other districts. It voted for Trump by fewer than 8 points in 2024, and it’s based around Dayton, which has many Democratic voters. “But he has been an excellent performer even in tough years, so he’s not as vulnerable as the partisan topline might suggest,” Kondik wrote. Republican Representative Michael Turner is a strong incumbent who has won by large margins in the past despite the district being only light red. He is facing a challenge from Democrat Kristina Knickerbocker, a veteran. Turner has drawn credible challenges in the past but has been able to withstand stronger Democratic environments. Other Rating Changes The other changes are in races that were already thought to be competitive. Democrats’ Chances of Taking Back House: Polls Democrats have led generic ballot polls throughout 2026, but some surveys showed a tighter margin that would suggest a blue ripple, rather than a wave. But that’s changing, with recent surveys giving Democrats an expanded lead, some showing a double-digit advantage. The latest poll from YouGov and The Economist gave Democrats a 12-point lead among 1,051 likely voters, 51 percent to 39 percent. Six percent were still undecided, and 3 percent said they would vote for another party. The poll highlights the GOP’s motivation problem. Among all registered voters, Democrats only led by 5 points, 44 percent to 39 percent. It was conducted from September 11 to 14, 2026. Democrats had a 7-point lead in the latest Reuters/Ipsos poll, 44 percent to 37 percent. It surveyed 896 registered voters from September 11 to 14, 2026. Meanwhile, The New York Times and Siena University released a poll giving Democrats a 9-point lead, 51 percent to 43 percent. It surveyed 1,503 likely voters from September 8 to 13, 2026. What Does Democrats’ Generic Ballot Lead Mean for the Midterms? It’s difficult to project exactly how a generic ballot lead would translate to the number of seat pickups for Democrats, especially as mid-decade redistricting has cast a level of uncertainty over the elections. But if that polling advantage holds up on Election Day, it could point to a more comfortable majority for Democrats. Here is a look at how recent elections have gone. What Happens Next Polls will continue to be closely watched ahead of November 3. Issues like the economy, cost of living, the Iran war, and AI could shape the contours of the midterms as candidates make their pitches to voters over the coming months. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jason Lemon and Gray R. Thomas
news.summary: Safe Republican seats shifted in Arkansas, Nevada, New York and Ohio, as Democrats expand their polling lead ahead of November.
news.author: Andrew Stanton

news.title: Democrats embraced AI’s growth before Trump came along; now, they want to slow it down
news.text: Some of the Democratic Party’s most prominent voices are pushing for tighter limits on artificial intelligence, including former President Barack Obama, who has joined calls for a slower pace of frontier AI development after years of Democratic leaders touting the technology’s economic and strategic potential. "We need government — and specifically our leaders in Washington — to get proactive in coming up with concrete proposals, laws and regulations that deal with serious safety concerns, anticipate AI’s impact on jobs and our kids and make sure that AI’s benefits are widely spread," Obama said in a statement Monday night. Obama’s latest comments put greater emphasis on slowing frontier AI development than his White House did in 2016, when his administration highlighted the technology’s economic potential while also warning about disruption and calling for policy responses. AI EXTINCTION WARNINGS DOMINATE HEADLINES AFTER EX-ANTHROPIC EMPLOYEE'S VIRAL POST Democrats have long paired enthusiasm for AI’s economic and strategic potential with warnings about its risks, but some of the party’s most prominent voices are now going further, calling for a slower pace of frontier AI development and tougher limits on how the technology is built and deployed. Attorney General Todd Blanche argued Tuesday that Democrats’ renewed focus on the potential risks of artificial intelligence should not be treated as "breaking news," suggesting the timing, months before the midterm elections, is politically significant. "Every Democrat senator suddenly races to a microphone to talk about AI after being eerily silent for months and months, a month. So, to talk about the timing of this as being nothing but an effort to influence the midterms, I shouldn't have to say that out loud, of course," said Blanche. The comments came as President Donald Trump has made rapid AI development and the data centers needed to power it a priority, while the administration promotes the technology’s potential economic benefits and faces growing political scrutiny over the cost and impact of expanding data-center infrastructure. Obama issued a statement Monday on X, writing that AI is "moving at lightning speed – and even faster than those who are engineering it can keep up with." "Given what we know about technology, we can’t stuff AI back in a box. But we can collectively determine how it's developed and how it’s used, rather than sitting back and letting AI and its fallout happen to us," he wrote. He called for regulation, saying choices to slow down should not be left up to the tech companies. Any "potential catastrophe will depend on the choices that we make right now," said Obama. ANTHROPIC CEO CALLS ON AI INDUSTRY TO SLOW DOWN TECH RACE, DRAWING SUPPORT FROM ELON MUSK, SAM ALTMAN In 2016, Obama’s White House touted AI’s potential to open new markets and drive progress across industries while warning about job disruption and broader safety and policy challenges. "Advances in AI technology hold incredible potential to help the United States stay on the cutting edge of innovation," the White House said in its December 2016 Artificial Intelligence, Automation, and the Economy report. "Advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI) technology and related fields have opened up new markets and new opportunities for progress in critical areas such as health, education, energy, economic inclusion, social welfare, and the environment. … AI should be welcomed for its potential economic benefits," the report added. Similarly, then-Vice President Kamala Harris said in January 2025 that "it is imperative that the United States remain the global leader on AI" as the Biden administration moved to speed up the buildout needed to support large-scale AI operations. The Biden administration announced an executive order aimed at accelerating AI infrastructure in the U.S., including large data centers and clean-energy projects, as the administration sought to keep the country ahead of its global competitors. Harris has also recently called for slowing the pace of frontier AI development, arguing that the technology is advancing at an "alarming speed" and urging Congress to establish stronger oversight and safety standards. "The frontier of artificial intelligence is advancing at an alarming speed. Over the weekend, industry leaders voiced support for an idea that the American people and many AI researchers in their own labs have been calling for: We must responsibly slow the pace of frontier AI development," she wrote. SEVEN-FIGURE BLITZ AS GOP EMBRACES PUSH TO COMPETE WITH CHINA IN BOOMING NEW TECH SPACE AI and data centers have quickly become a major midterm issue, as concerns over electricity costs, jobs and the rapid buildout draw increasing attention from candidates in both parties. news.text:
Gov. Gavin Newsom is slipping in 2028 presidential polls, as other Democrats pick up steam.

A new Bowling Green State University/YouGov poll found Newsom had dipped to third-place pick for the Democratic nominee with 14% support. That’s behind former VP Kamala Harris (17%) and former Biden Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg (16%).

Newsom led the pack in a February YouGov poll and has typically been in the top 2 with Harris. He told CNN this week he won’t launch his White House bid if Harris, a fellow Californian, puts her hat in the ring for a third try at the presidency, citing “mutually assured destruction.”

The latest poll, conducted Aug. 25 through Sept. 1, shows Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) gaining momentum. 

The Squad rep is tied with Newsom in third place at 14%, followed by Sen. Mark Kelly (D-AZ) at 10%. 

AOC said in an August interview that she “hasn’t ruled out the possibility” of running in 2028, and that she’s focused on winning the 2026 midterms.

Buttigieg’s support has also grown this year, as Newsom falters. Kelly has also been making early presidential moves by visiting early voting states and raising his profile.

YouGov’s latest September poll was conducted with 1200 US registered voters, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3.3 percentage points. It did not survey voters about Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-GA), who is polling favorably in other surveys. 

The Post reached out to Harris’s, Newsom’s, AOC’s, Buttigieg’s, and Kelly’s offices and did not receive an immediate response.

news.title: Gavin Newsom Is Back on Top of One 2028 List. Does It Mean Anything?
news.text:
In veteran political reporter Mark Halperin's July rankings of potential 2028 Democratic presidential nominees, Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) was rising, while Gov. Gavin Newsom (D-Calif.) was losing momentum. Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) candidates had just achieved huge victories in New York and Colorado primaries the previous month, and Halperin declared that the toughest thing to do in Democratic politics was to stop a socialist from becoming the presidential nominee.

Newsom slipped from first place to second place in August. Now, in Halperin's September rankings, he's back on top. What changed?

Halperin compiles his monthly rankings by asking more than 60 analysts, mostly Democrats, whom they think is most likely to become the party's 2028 nominee. Despite placing Newsom first in July, Halperin believed the governor would ultimately decide not to run because he is the subject of U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) investigations.

Sanders, who ranked third in July behind Newsom and Gov. Josh Shapiro (D-Pa.), was one of three candidates in Halperin's top eight that month from what he called the "Mamdani wing of the Democratic Party." Halperin was bullish on the Vermont senator because he believed the Democratic establishment was weaker than ever and that candidates from the establishment wing realized they had to "cater to the progressive wing."

That brings us back to Newsom. Halperin now thinks the governor has figured out how to do just that: appeal to the Democratic Party's socialist wing. He points to a Sept. 7 PBS interview Newsom gave in South Carolina in which he was asked where he stands on the DSA. Newsom answered: "If it's about more money in your pocket, lowering costs ... getting money out of politics and ... about Medicare for all, I think we're pretty aligned." While most Republicans can't listen to a word the hand-gesticulating governor says without thinking "phony," Halperin praised the answer's "sophistication":

I've not heard Chuck Schumer, Hakeem Jeffries, or any other potential presidentials talk about a big tent with such confidence and clarity as Newsom did in that one answer. And that's a testament not only to the prospect that he can win some of those votes, even if there's a socialist in the race if he runs, and that he can keep the party united the way Hillary Clinton struggled to do in 2016, part of why she didn't beat Donald Trump, but that he has a lot of savvy and a lot of confidence.And people underrate the ability that he has to think through and speak. It's kind of ironic because one of the biggest raps against him is he's inauthentic. A lot of people say that about him. That's not what I think about him.

What about another potential candidate whom so many find inauthentic: Kamala Harris? Newsom recently told Jake Tapper while the two were fly-fishing that he wouldn't run for president if the former vice president decided to run because it would be "mutual assured destruction." Halperin took that mysterious answer into consideration but ultimately kept Newsom at number one. Although Harris, like Newsom, would be able to raise a lot of money, he agrees with those who believe she won't run. For that reason, she lands at number six on his list.

Gov. Shapiro, who appears poised to cruise to reelection, is another candidate who can raise money. Halperin still has him in the number two position, but last I checked, he's still Jewish, so I think that's way too high for a party with an out-of-control antisemitism problem.

Being gay and short may be less of a problem than being Jewish. Halperin acknowledges that many people write off Pete Buttigieg, number three on the list, because of those two characteristics, but he thinks he's a strong contender for three reasons: He knows how to campaign, win votes, and build coalitions. The big question remains whether he can win over black voters, which he wasn't able to do the last time he ran.

These names make up the so-called "establishment" wing of the Democratic Party, although the establishment and socialist wings are becoming increasingly difficult to distinguish. As Victor Davis Hanson notes, "Democratic Socialists became mainstream largely by imitating an increasingly socialist Democratic Party."

 Related: Bernie Rising: Is Sanders Becoming a 2028 Frontrunner?

As for the more unabashedly socialist candidates, Halperin ranks Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y., 14th District) at number four, ahead of Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) at number seven, although he is not certain that she'll run — despite speculation concerning her decision to freeze her eggs.

And I continue to believe that one of the biggest moments that's coming in the presidential nomination fight for the Democrats is when AOC and Bernie sit down and have conversations, which I suspect they'll do right after the midterms. Which one of them's going to run? And if neither of them's going to run, the Democrats are going to face a problem. But I believe that if she does run, she will be the consensus socialist choice—progressive choice—even though a lot of progressives think, ironically, she's too moderate.

The takeaway from Halperin's admittedly way-too-early horse-race prognostication is that some of the leading contenders might not even enter the race.

One name we can rule out, however, is Zohran Mamdani. If the names on Halperin's list are too depressing for you to contemplate, at least take comfort in the fact that the New York City mayor isn't among them.

news.title: Trump accuses Democrats of mishandling his assassination attempt probe
news.text:
US President Donald Trump has claimed that an FBI probe into his attempted assassination in July 2024 was deliberately mishandled as part of a “Democrat plot” to prevent him from winning a second term. He also referred to “new info” that supposedly appeared in the case, but provided no details.

In 2024, Trump, then the Republican presidential candidate, narrowly escaped death at a campaign rally in Butler, Pennsylvania, when a 20-year-old man fired shots from a rooftop, grazing Trump’s ear and killing one attendee and injuring two others.

Trump claimed at the time that President Joe Biden and his Democratic rival, Kamala Harris, were partly to blame as they allegedly made it more difficult for the Secret Service to protect him, while peddling rhetoric that could have encouraged the shooter.

The would-be assassin, Thomas M. Crooks, was killed by the US Secret Service. An internal review released later that year concluded that the Secret Service made multiple mistakes ahead of the shooting.

“Everybody knows the Crooked Joe Biden FBI didn’t do what they should have with respect to the Lunatic who shot me in Butler,” Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social on Tuesday.

He also claimed that “most of the information [on the case] was missing, altered, corrupted, or gone” by the time he took office in January 2025. “This was all a Democrat Plot, to get me out of the Election, that failed,” the president stated, adding that some new information on the case had emerged recently, but provided no details.

Trump also blamed former FBI Director Christopher Wray for mishandling the probe and maintained he “should pay a price for the way he handled this assassination attempt, and certainly for the things he said.”

Wray, who was nominated by Trump himself during his first term in office, stated that his agency did not find any accomplices of the shooter during testimony to the House Judiciary Committee. He also said it was unclear if Trump had been hit directly by a bullet or by shrapnel, provoking sharp criticism from Trump at the time. Wray resigned before Trump’s inauguration in January 2025.

The current FBI director, Kash Patel, told the Senate Judiciary Committee on Tuesday that his agency looked into Crooks’ possible connection to any accomplices but found none. “We found no evidence that that individual was literally even speaking to any other human being other than his parents, who he resided with,” he said.

Attorney General Todd Blanche mentioned during the same hearing that new information related to the case had surfaced recently. “It is new information about the shooter and about his background, about his history and that’s stuff that we didn’t know before,” he said while refusing to elaborate.

Trump has been targeted in several assassination attempts. Two months after the July 2024 incident, a pro-Ukraine activist was arrested after being spotted with a rifle near Trump’s golf course in Florida. He was later found guilty of trying to assassinate Trump.

In April 2026, the president and First Lady Melania Trump were rushed from the Washington Hilton after gunfire broke out at the White House Correspondents’ Association Dinner. The suspect, Cole Tomas Allen, was later charged with attempting to assassinate the president as well.

news.title: How Kamala Harris’ campaign lied about Beyonce, Taylor Swift and Bad Bunny to attract and exploit crowds
news.text:
For years, Lindy Li was an extremely active member of the Democratic Party. A former financial analyst, she ran for Congress in 2018 but lost in the Democratic primary. She went on to become a key fundraiser for the DNC, raising millions for Joe Biden’s presidential campaign in 2020 and Kamala Harris’ in 2024. But, in the wake of Harris’ defeat, dismayed with what she’d seen and how money had been spent, she had a highly publicized break from the party, which she details in her new book, “Unburdened: A Former Democrat Insider’s Shocking Account of Political Power, Betrayal, and Party Collapse” (Harper, Sept. 22). “I don’t think I could have lived with myself had I not told the truth,” she recently told Fox News. In this excerpt, she writes of how the Harris campaign lied about celebrities such as Beyonce and Taylor Swift to attract and exploit crowds.

Beyoncé will perform on the final night of the convention!

Just kidding — that was just a lie to pack the stadium for Kamala’s acceptance speech.

Deceit slithered through Chicago like Dementors from “Harry Potter,” chilling the air as fifty thousand delegates, alternates, volunteers and press descended upon Carl Sandburg’s “Hog Butcher for the World.” 

As a member of the National Finance Committee, I was ushered in as a VIP, gliding from our hotel to the United Center in a private shuttle that looped through the city’s veins.

But the moment Beyoncé failed to take the convention stage, disillusionment spilled into plain view. True to form, Team B.O.C.H. — the name I’d given Biden, Obama, Clinton and Harris — botched the optics with spectacular ineptitude, courting worldwide ridicule and accusations of deceit. 

Older Americans may not comprehend the power this pop demigod wields over the liberal faithful, but by willfully fanning the flames of the wildfire rumors, they effectively swore to the surging throngs — chiefly younger voters, an indispensable electoral force — that Queen Bey would serenade the masses. When she didn’t, the betrayal clanged with cataclysmic force, raw, ruthless, and ragingly ruinous. Harris face-planted before the very voters she needed most.

The singer P!nk wasn’t a big enough artist to fill Beyoncé’s towering stilettos. Alex observed that historians would pinpoint the Beyoncé debacle as the tipping point, the moment the campaign’s sugar high crashed into a brutal hangover, highlighting Harris’s ineptitude at political pageantry and her inability to follow through on her massive promises. In politics, as in life, perception is reality; the court of public opinion either dooms or deifies.

The DNC’s boneheaded showmanship hit a new low in Houston at a high-profile rally on Oct. 25. Less than two weeks ahead of the election, they once again dangled Beyoncé like forbidden fruit, only to snatch it away a second time, igniting a righteous rage that rippled through the ranks. Queen Bey, loved for her anthems, not her analyses, gave a speech that no one wanted. She had performed for Clinton in 2016, only for Trump’s win to splatter egg on her sequins. Perhaps she was done wagering her crown on another politician. When Harris took the stage after Bey’s letdown, she was greeted by furious howls, serpents of humanity streaming toward the exits. Team Harris wielded celebrities as crowd-wrangling bait, a tacit admission

In the campaign’s ebbing final hours, a VIP summons thunked in my inbox: an invitation to Vice President Harris’s valedictory rally, promising a lineup of mystery superstars, right here in Philadelphia, the aorta of the swing states. For a full week, Kamala’s rumor factory cranked at full throttle, recycling the playbook they had used to generate hype for Beyoncé’s twice-teased, twice-thwarted appearances: first at the convention, then at the Houston rally. The stage was set for history. Or, as it turned out, for the most expensive karaoke night in American political memory.

To build mystique around their pièce de résistance, Kamala’s hype arsonists torched what little credibility they had left in one sun-kissed conflagration of rumor: Taylor Swift, Pennsylvania’s prodigal daughter, was allegedly descending from the pop-star heavens in a blaze of sequins and voter registration forms to electrify a race that had flatlined for weeks.

The night before the election, Fox News journalist Jacqui Heinrich suggested to me that it would be Taylor. Citing his own Vatican-level infallibility, a high-ranking Biden White House official said with absolute certainty that it was going to be Bad Bunny. Campaign czars swore it would be a chart-incinerating rock star, not a recently dumped has-been desperate to scrape together more sales on the worst-reviewed album of the year.

A fellow megabundler pinged his jealously guarded hunch: Beyoncé, stung by the backlash to her two non-performances and desiring redemption, would make the third time the charm.

Theories swirled like fanfic plot twists: Why Taylor? Home-state halo. Bey? Redemption arc. Bad Bunny? Youthquake bait. Pop’s pantheon had to descend — it simply had to. No universe existed where Kamala would shaft young Americans yet again, belly-flopping before the nation’s glare, with the entire globe thirsting like coyotes for the next overlong heehaw or word salad.

So, you can imagine the universal disappointment when the mystery guest was unmasked once more as Katy Perry, ready to bumble through the songs she wrote with an accused sex pest to a crowd of single-issue #MeToo voters. This was a con executed with sociopathic detachment. They dangled Taylor, Beyoncé, and Bad Bunny overhead like manna, luring thirty thousand shivering masochists onto frozen concrete, and the internet flambéed itself in a frenzy of speculation.

By the time Katy bounced out waving a sparkler nobody wanted, the footage was already cut, the headlines were locked, and the dopamine had been strip-mined. But instead of a single villain, there was a syndicate of deceit, each pocketing a succulent slice of the scam. Kamala, Queen Con, reaped rivers of rapturous ink and Instagram idolatry, snagging her Rocky moment. Her optics-obsessed staffers got their crowds. Media moguls milked the ad dollars. Influencers surfed the clickbait tsunami.
